title: Malabsorption Syndromes
subject: Medicine
summary: Malabsorption is the impaired digestion or absorption of nutrients, leading to weight loss, diarrhoea and micronutrient deficiencies. In low‑resource settings tropical infections, HIV and TB are common causes. Diagnosis relies on clinical clues and targeted tests, often with limited laboratory support.

sections.p: Malabsorption refers to the failure of the gastrointestinal tract to adequately digest or absorb macronutrients, micronutrients, electrolytes, or water, despite normal intake.
b: Key diagnostic criteria: chronic diarrhoea (>4 weeks), weight loss >5% body weight, steatorrhea, and laboratory evidence of nutrient loss.
Rule out pancreatic insufficiency, bile acid diarrhoea and overt infection first.

sections.p: Severity is graded by clinical impact and laboratory deficits.
b: Mild: <5% weight loss, normal serum albumin, no electrolyte disturbance.
Moderate: 5‑10% weight loss, mild hypoalbuminaemia (30‑35 g/L), mild anaemia.
Severe: >10% weight loss, albumin <30 g/L, severe electrolyte or vitamin deficiencies, or failure to thrive in children.

sections.p: Causes are grouped by anatomic level: luminal, mucosal, and post‑absorptive.
b: Luminal: Giardia lamblia, Strongyloides, chronic helminths, tropical sprue, HIV enteropathy.
Mucosal: Celiac disease (rare in East Africa), Crohn’s disease, intestinal TB, radiation enteritis.
Post‑absorptive: Chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, bile‑acid deficiency after ileal resection.

sections.p: Patients present with chronic diarrhoea (often fatty and foul‑smelling), weight loss, abdominal bloating, and signs of specific deficiencies.
b: Fat‑soluble vitamin deficiency → night blindness (vit A), easy bruising (vit K).
Iron or folate deficiency → microcytic or macrocytic anaemia.
Calcium oxalate kidney stones from fat malabsorption (enteric hyperoxaluria).

sections.p: Select tests that answer a specific clinical question; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Detect luminal parasites (Giardia, Strongyloides) → positive result confirms infectious cause.
Assess severity; hypoalbuminaemia <30 g/L signals severe protein loss.

t.a: Serum vitamin levels (A, D, E, K) if available
t.b: Identify specific micronutrient deficiencies; treat accordingly.
Differentiates mucosal from pancreatic causes; low serum D‑xylose suggests mucosal disease.
Looks for pancreatic calcifications, biliary dilatation, or ascites when CT is unavailable.

sections.p: Unrecognised severe malabsorption can rapidly become life‑threatening.
b: Severe electrolyte disturbance (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia).
Profound hypoalbuminaemia leading to oedema or anasarca.
Vitamin K deficiency causing coagulopathy.
Enteric hyperoxaluria with renal colic or acute kidney injury.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then replace lost nutrients and support gut function.
b: Antiparasitics (metronidazole for Giardia, ivermectin for Strongyloides) – eradicate luminal infection.
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics for tropical sprue (tetracycline) – reduce bacterial overgrowth.
Pancreatic enzyme replacement (pancrelipase) for pancreatic insufficiency – improves fat digestion.
High‑calorie, low‑fat diet with medium‑chain triglycerides – easier absorption.
Supplement vitamins A, D, E, K, B12, iron, folate as indicated – correct deficiencies.
Avoid high‑oxalate foods (spinach, nuts) when fat malabsorption present – reduce kidney stone risk.

sections.p: Monitor weight, nutritional labs and symptom resolution; educate on hygiene and safe water.
b: Re‑check weight and stool frequency every 2‑4 weeks until stable.
Repeat stool microscopy after treatment to confirm eradication.
Vaccinate against rotavirus and hepatitis A/B where available to reduce secondary infections.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic malabsorption but have different pathophysiology.
b: Irritable bowel syndrome – functional pain without nutrient loss.
Chronic pancreatitis with pain‑dominant presentation – may have malabsorption but requires imaging confirmation.
Normal serum albumin can be falsely reassuring in early disease; weight loss is more sensitive.
Stool fat may appear normal if collection is incomplete; use clinical steatorrhea clues.

faq.q: Why does fat malabsorption cause calcium oxalate stones?
faq.a: Unabsorbed fatty acids bind calcium, leaving free oxalate to be absorbed and excreted in urine, forming stones.

faq.q: Can HIV alone cause malabsorption without opportunistic infection?
faq.a: Yes, HIV enteropathy directly damages enterocytes, leading to villous blunting and nutrient loss.

faq.q: Is a low‑fat diet always recommended?
faq.a: Low‑fat diets help when fat malabsorption is severe; however, adequate calories must be provided via medium‑chain triglycerides.

exam: What bedside clues would make you suspect malabsorption in a patient with chronic diarrhoea? — Look for steatorrhea, weight loss, abdominal distension, and signs of vitamin deficiencies.

How would you differentiate tropical sprue from Giardia infection using limited tests? — Perform stool microscopy; Giardia shows cysts/ trophozoites, while sprue often has normal stool but responds to tetracycline.

A patient with HIV presents with diarrhoea and weight loss but negative stool studies. What is your next step? — Consider HIV enteropathy; start empirical antiretroviral optimisation and give broad micronutrient supplementation.

When is pancreatic enzyme replacement indicated, and why avoid high‑fat meals initially? — Indicated in pancreatic insufficiency confirmed by low fecal elastase; high‑fat meals worsen steatorrhea until enzymes are effective.
Explain why serum albumin may be normal early in malabsorption and how you would still assess severity. — Albumin has a long half‑life; use weight trend, stool volume, and electrolyte panels instead.

A child with chronic diarrhoea has normal stool microscopy but low vitamin A. What condition is most likely and how to treat? — Tropical sprue; give tetracycline for 3 weeks plus vitamin A and other micronutrient repletion.
What red‑flag symptom mandates urgent referral in a malabsorption patient? — Severe electrolyte disturbance or rapid weight loss >10% in two weeks.
Why are medium‑chain triglycerides preferred in fat malabsorption? — They are absorbed directly into the portal circulation without requiring micelle formation.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
b: Key history questions: duration and character of diarrhoea (frequency, consistency, colour, odour, presence of blood/mucus), associated abdominal pain, bloating, nausea, vomiting, appetite, recent travel, diet, alcohol intake, previous GI surgery, family history of GI disease, and symptoms of nutritional deficiencies (fatigue, bruising, bleeding, night blindness, bone pain, neu
Weight loss: quantify percentage loss over a defined period (e.g., >5% in 6-12 months, or >10% in 6 months).

Ask about symptoms suggestive of specific deficiencies: easy bruising/bleeding (Vit K), night blindness/poor vision (Vit A), bone pain/fractures (Vit D/Calcium), fatigue/dyspnoea (iron/folate), neurological symptoms (Vit B12).
Inquire about symptoms of underlying conditions: joint pain (Crohn's, coeliac), skin rashes (coeliac, dermatitis herpetiformis), fever/night sweats (TB, infection).

Abdominal examination: Inspection for distension or scars. Palpation for tenderness, masses, or organomegaly. Percussion for ascites (dullness) or tympany. Auscultation for bowel sounds (hyperactive in diarrhoea, reduced in ileus).

t.b: Inspection: visible generalised or localised swelling. Positive if present. Indicates gas, fluid, or mass. Bedside tests cannot quantify the cause or volume.
Palpation: localised or generalised pain on pressure. Positive if elicited. Indicates inflammation or irritation. Bedside tests cannot determine the specific cause of inflammation.

Percussion: patient lies on side, percuss from midline to flank. Dullness shifts to dependent flank, resonance to upper flank. Positive if shifting occurs. Indicates ascites. Bedside tests cannot differentiate transudate from exudate.

Percussion: patient/assistant presses hand firmly on midline abdomen, tap flank. Positive if a fluid impulse is felt across the abdomen. Indicates significant ascites. Bedside tests cannot determine the cause of ascites.

Inspection of perianal area for fissures, fistulae, or skin tags. Palpation for masses or tenderness. Assessment of stool colour and presence of blood. Positive if abnormalities found. Bedside tests cannot confirm mucosal pathology or internal disease.

b: Diagnosis is confirmed by a combination of clinical features (chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, steatorrhea), laboratory evidence (e.g., quantitative fecal fat test, D-xylose test), and response to treatment.
Severity of malabsorption is assessed based on the degree of weight loss, nutritional deficiencies, and impact on organ function.
Red‑flag symptoms: persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, high fever, bloody diarrhoea, signs of dehydration, acute kidney injury, or profound electrolyte imbalance.
Persistent weight loss (>5% in 6-12 months, or >10% in 6 months) is a key indicator of significant malabsorption.
Severe electrolyte disturbance (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia) requires urgent correction and investigation.
Profound hypoalbuminemia (albumin <30 g/L) leads to oedema or anasarca and indicates severe protein loss.
Vitamin K deficiency causing coagulopathy (prolonged PT/INR) mandates urgent vitamin K replacement and investigation for the cause.
Enteric hyperoxaluria with renal colic or acute kidney injury from fat malabsorption requires aggressive fluid management and calcium intake modification.

t.b: Points to it: Chronic diarrhoea, bloating, abdominal pain, often alternating with constipation. No significant weight loss or nutritional deficiencies. How to separate: IBS symptoms are typically related to bowel habit and pain, without objective evidence of malabsorption (normal fecal fat, D-xylose).

b: Initial assessment and stabilization: Address immediate life threats such as severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalances (especially hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia), and profound hypoalbuminaemia. Correct severe anaemia (Hb <7 g/dL or symptomatic anaemia) – consider blood transfusion.

Nutritional support: Commence with easily digestible nutrients. Medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs) are preferred as they are absorbed directly into the portal circulation without requiring bile salts or pancreatic enzymes. Gradually introduce long-chain triglycerides as tolerance improves.

Empirical treatment for common infections: In endemic areas, empirical treatment for parasitic infections like Giardia lamblia (metronidazole) and Strongyloides (ivermectin) is often warranted, especially if diagnostic facilities are limited. For tropical sprue, a combination of tetracycline and folic acid is the first-line therapy.

Specific treatment of underlying cause: Once a diagnosis is established, target the specific aetiology. This may involve antiparasitic agents, antibiotics for bacterial overgrowth, immunosuppressants for inflammatory conditions (e.g., Crohn's disease), or surgical intervention for obstructive causes.

Replacement of deficiencies: Systematically correct deficiencies in vitamins (fat-soluble A, D, E, K; water-soluble B vitamins, especially B12 and folate) and minerals (iron, calcium, zinc, magnesium).

Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT): For pancreatic insufficiency, start oral pancreatic enzymes. These should be taken with meals and snacks. Dosing is adjusted based on symptoms and stool consistency. Concurrent use of acid suppression (e.g., PPIs) may enhance efficacy.

Monitoring and follow-up: Regular clinical assessment for weight gain, resolution of diarrhoea, and improvement in nutritional status. Monitor relevant laboratory parameters (e.g., albumin, haemoglobin, vitamin levels, electrolytes) to assess treatment response and identify ongoing deficiencies.

Escalation and referral: Refer patients with severe, refractory malabsorption, significant complications (e.g., renal failure, coagulopathy), or those failing to respond to initial management to a specialist centre for further investigation and management.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do

t.b: Adverse effects: Nausea, metallic taste, peripheral neuropathy (with prolonged use), disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol. Action: Counsel patients to avoid alcohol during and for 48 hours after treatment. Monitor for neurological symptoms with prolonged courses.

Adverse effects: Dizziness, headache, rash, potential for severe neurological reactions in patients with Loa loa co-infection (Massive Cutaneous Adverse Events - MCRAE). Action: Screen for Loa loa if prevalent in the region before administration. Monitor for adverse reactions.

Adverse effects: Photosensitivity, gastrointestinal upset, tooth discolouration in children, vaginal candidiasis. Action: Advise patients to avoid excessive sun exposure and use sunscreen. Take with adequate fluid to prevent oesophageal irritation. Avoid in pregnancy and young children.

Adverse effects: Constipation, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, hyperuricosuria (rare). Action: Ensure adequate hydration. Adjust dose if symptoms persist. Monitor for signs of hyperuricosuria (e.g., kidney stones) if on high doses for prolonged periods.

b: Severe malnutrition and cachexia: Characterized by profound weight loss (>10% body weight), muscle wasting, and impaired immune function. Escalation: Requires aggressive nutritional support, often including parenteral nutrition if enteral feeding is insufficient.

Electrolyte disturbances: Hypokalaemia can lead to cardiac arrhythmias and muscle weakness. Hyponatraemia can cause confusion and seizures. Escalation: Requires urgent electrolyte correction, often with intravenous fluids and close monitoring.

Osteoporosis and fractures: Due to malabsorption of calcium and vitamin D. Escalation: Requires calcium and vitamin D supplementation, bone density monitoring, and consideration of bisphosphonates if severe.

Coagulopathy: Vitamin K deficiency leads to impaired synthesis of clotting factors, increasing the risk of bleeding. Escalation: Requires vitamin K replacement and monitoring of prothrombin time/INR. Urgent management if active bleeding occurs.

Renal calculi: Enteric hyperoxaluria from fat malabsorption can lead to calcium oxalate stones. Escalation: Requires increased fluid intake, calcium supplementation (to bind oxalate in the gut), and dietary modification.

Neurological complications: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, and cognitive impairment. Vitamin A deficiency can lead to night blindness and xerophthalmia. Escalation: Requires specific vitamin replacement and neurological assessment.

Failure to thrive in children: Persistent malabsorption in children leads to poor growth, developmental delay, and increased susceptibility to infections. Escalation: Requires multidisciplinary team approach including paediatric gastroenterologists and dietitians.

HIV infection: HIV enteropathy can cause malabsorption at any CD4 count. Opportunistic infections (e.g., Cryptosporidium, Microsporidium) are also common causes of diarrhoea and malabsorption. Management requires treating the underlying HIV and any concurrent infections.
Tuberculosis (TB): Intestinal TB can present with malabsorption, mimicking other causes. Diagnosis can be challenging. Management requires standard anti-TB therapy, which may need to be prolonged.

Malnutrition: Pre-existing malnutrition exacerbates malabsorption and impairs recovery. It also increases susceptibility to infections. Management requires careful nutritional rehabilitation and addressing the cause of malabsorption.

Pregnancy: Increased physiological demands can unmask or worsen malabsorption. Certain investigations and treatments may be contraindicated. Management requires careful consideration of maternal and fetal well-being, with safer alternatives for drugs.

Diabetes Mellitus: Autonomic neuropathy can affect gut motility, contributing to malabsorption. Certain medications used in diabetes can also affect gut function. Management requires optimizing glycaemic control and considering drug effects.

Drugs and herbal remedies: Many medications (e.g., metformin, antibiotics, laxatives) and herbal preparations can cause diarrhoea or malabsorption. A thorough drug history is crucial. Management involves identifying and discontinuing offending agents where possible.

Alcohol abuse: Chronic alcohol use can lead to pancreatic damage (chronic pancreatitis) and direct mucosal injury, causing maldigestion and malabsorption. Management involves alcohol cessation and addressing pancreatic insufficiency.

Renal or liver failure: These conditions can affect nutrient metabolism and excretion, and may be associated with secondary gastrointestinal issues. Management requires addressing the primary organ failure and supportive care for malabsorption.

Age extremes (very young and elderly): Infants have immature digestive systems, making them prone to malabsorption. The elderly may have reduced digestive capacity, altered gut motility, and polypharmacy, increasing their risk. Management needs to be tailored to age-specific physiological changes and risks.

Children: Malabsorption can lead to failure to thrive, developmental delay, and rickets. Investigations need to be adapted for paediatric use. Management focuses on nutritional rehabilitation and addressing the specific cause, with careful monitoring of growth.

Pregnancy: Nutritional deficiencies can affect both mother and fetus. Investigations like endoscopy or biopsies may be deferred if possible. Treatment choices must consider teratogenicity; metronidazole is generally avoided in the first trimester for giardiasis.

Elderly: May have reduced digestive enzyme production, altered gut motility, and polypharmacy, increasing the risk of malabsorption. Investigations should be approached cautiously. Management focuses on optimizing nutrition and simplifying medication regimens.

People with HIV: Malabsorption is common due to HIV enteropathy or opportunistic infections. Management requires addressing the underlying HIV infection with antiretroviral therapy and treating any specific enteric pathogens.

Low-resource settings: Diagnostic facilities are often limited. Management relies heavily on clinical assessment, empirical treatment for common infections (e.g., Giardia, Strongyloides), and nutritional support. Stool microscopy for parasites is a key bedside tool.

facts: Rapid weight loss: >5% in 6-12 months or >10% in 6 months.
Serum albumin: <30 g/L indicates severe hypoalbuminaemia.
Hb <7 g/dL or symptomatic anaemia: consider blood transfusion.
Tropical sprue treatment: tetracycline and folic acid.

vivas.q: A 45-year-old female presents with persistent diarrhea, weight loss, and suspected malabsorption. A duodenal biopsy is stained with Congo red, showing orange-red deposits that display apple-green birefringence under polarized light. What is the most likely diagnosis?
vivas.a: This finding is pathognomonic for amyloidosis. Amyloid deposition in the small bowel can lead to malabsorption by interfering with mucosal integrity and function.

vivas.q: A 45-year-old man presents with chronic steatorrhea and abdominal pain. Endoscopic workup reveals exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. Which digestive enzyme deficiency is the primary cause of his lipid malabsorption?
vivas.a: Lipase deficiency is the primary cause of lipid malabsorption in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. Lipase is essential for breaking down triglycerides into absorbable fatty acids and monoglycerides.

vivas.q: A patient with an ileal resection develops severe vitamin B12 deficiency and bile salt malabsorption. Which specific transporter mechanism in the terminal ileum is disrupted by this surgical intervention?
vivas.a: The intrinsic factor-vitamin B12 receptor complex (also known as cubilin-amnionless complex) is disrupted, preventing B12 absorption. Additionally, the apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter (ASBT) is disrupted, leading to bile salt malabsorption.

vivas.q: A patient with fat malabsorption secondary to Crohn's disease exhibits areflexia and hemolytic anemia. Which fat-soluble vitamin acts primarily as an intracellular antioxidant?
vivas.a: Vitamin E (tocopherol) acts primarily as an intracellular antioxidant. Its deficiency can lead to neurological symptoms like areflexia and hemolytic anemia due to oxidative damage to red blood cell membranes.

vivas.q: A patient presents with chronic malabsorption and foul-smelling steatorrhea. Duodenal biopsy confirms Giardia lamblia infection. How does this parasite primarily induce malabsorption without invading the mucosal epithelium?
vivas.a: Giardia lamblia causes malabsorption by adhering to the brush border of the small intestine, forming a physical barrier. This interferes with nutrient absorption, damages microvilli, and can induce inflammation, leading to impaired enzyme function and increased permeability.

vivas.q: An infant who underwent a massive bowel resection for gangrenous intussusception develops severe malabsorption and fluid balance issues postoperatively. Which complication of surgical management is this infant most likely experiencing?
vivas.a: This infant is most likely experiencing short bowel syndrome. This condition results from extensive loss of small intestine, leading to inadequate surface area for nutrient and fluid absorption.

vivas.q: A 6-year-old child presents with chronic intermittent abdominal pain, malabsorption, and recurrent episodes of vomiting. An upper GI contrast study reveals that the duodenojejunal junction lies to the right of the midline. What is the most likely diagnosis?
vivas.a: This finding suggests intestinal malrotation. Malrotation can lead to chronic abdominal pain, malabsorption due to altered anatomy and potential intermittent volvulus, and recurrent vomiting.

vivas.q: A patient with systemic sclerosis presents with severe gastrointestinal dysmotility and malabsorption. What is the underlying histological change in the bowel wall?
vivas.a: The underlying histological change is fibrosis and atrophy of the smooth muscle layers, along with vascular changes and neural degeneration. This leads to impaired peristalsis and nutrient transit.

vivas.q: Distinguish between maldigestion and malabsorption in the context of chronic diarrhea.
vivas.a: Maldigestion is the impaired breakdown of nutrients into absorbable forms, often due to enzyme deficiencies (e.g., pancreatic insufficiency). Malabsorption is the impaired uptake of digested nutrients across the intestinal mucosa into the bloodstream or lymphatics (e.g., celiac disease).

vivas.q: A patient died following prolonged cholestasis. On post-mortem examination, the skin showed evidence of xanthomas and the gastrointestinal tract revealed signs of severe malabsorption. Explain the underlying mechanisms for malabsorption in this context.
vivas.a: Prolonged cholestasis leads to reduced bile flow into the intestine. Bile salts are crucial for emulsifying dietary fats and forming micelles, which are necessary for fat-soluble vitamin absorption. Their deficiency results in severe fat and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption.

vivas.q: In a post-mortem examination, you note signs of severe fat malabsorption in the gastrointestinal tract. Briefly describe the two primary functions of bile that are essential for normal digestion and excretion.
vivas.a: Bile's primary functions are: 1) Emulsification of dietary fats in the small intestine, increasing their surface area for enzymatic digestion by lipase. 2) Formation of micelles with digested fats and fat-soluble vitamins, facilitating their transport to the intestinal brush border for absorption. Bile also aids in cholesterol and bilirubin excretion.

vivas.q: A patient with chronic liver disease presented with generalized pruritus, pale stools, and dark urine prior to death. Post-mortem examination showed evidence of significant bile retention. What is the clinical term for this condition, and how does it relate to malabsorption?
vivas.a: The clinical term is cholestasis. Bile retention leads to a lack of bile salts in the intestine, impairing fat emulsification and micelle formation. This results in severe fat malabsorption, causing pale stools (steatorrhea) and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins.

vivas.q: What bedside clues would make you suspect malabsorption in a patient with chronic diarrhoea?
vivas.a: Key clues include chronic, often foul-smelling, fatty diarrhoea (steatorrhea), significant unintentional weight loss, abdominal bloating or distension, muscle wasting, and signs of specific nutrient deficiencies like pallor (anaemia), easy bruising (vitamin K), or night blindness (vitamin A).

vivas.q: How would you differentiate tropical sprue from Giardia infection using limited tests?
vivas.a: Stool microscopy for Giardia cysts/trophozoites is key for Giardia. If negative, a therapeutic trial of metronidazole for Giardia can be considered. For tropical sprue, a D-xylose absorption test showing impaired absorption, along with a good response to broad-spectrum antibiotics (tetracycline and folic acid), would support the diagnosis.

vivas.q: A patient with HIV presents with diarrhoea and weight loss but negative stool studies. What is your next step in investigation?
vivas.a: Consider HIV enteropathy, opportunistic infections not detected by routine stool studies (e.g., Cryptosporidium, Microsporidia, CMV), or other causes like intestinal TB. Further steps include upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsy, colonoscopy with biopsies, and specific PCR tests for opportunistic pathogens if available.

vivas.q: When is pancreatic enzyme replacement indicated, and why avoid high-fat meals initially?
vivas.a: Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) is indicated for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency causing steatorrhea and malabsorption. Patients should not necessarily avoid high-fat meals; instead, PERT should be dosed appropriately to allow for digestion of fat, often requiring higher doses with fatty meals.

vivas.q: Explain why serum albumin may be normal early in malabsorption and how you would still assess severity.
vivas.a: Serum albumin has a long half-life, so levels may remain normal early in malabsorption despite ongoing protein loss. Severity is still assessed by the degree of weight loss, other specific nutrient deficiencies (e.g., iron, folate, fat-soluble vitamins), and clinical impact on the patient's functional status.

vivas.q: A child with chronic diarrhoea has normal stool microscopy but low vitamin A. What condition is most likely?
vivas.a: Given normal stool microscopy and low vitamin A (a fat-soluble vitamin), conditions causing fat malabsorption are most likely. This could include pancreatic insufficiency, tropical sprue, or less commonly, celiac disease (though rare in East Africa).

mcqs.q: A 30-year-old patient presents with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and abdominal pain. Stool microscopy shows numerous Giardia lamblia trophozoites. Which of the following is the primary mechanism by which Giardia causes malabsorption?
o: Invasion and destruction of intestinal enterocytes.
Production of toxins that damage the intestinal villi.
Induction of severe systemic inflammation leading to gut dysmotility.
Adherence to the brush border, creating a physical barrier and damaging microvilli.
mcqs.e: Giardia lamblia adheres to the brush border of the small intestine, forming a physical barrier that interferes with nutrient absorption and causes microvillus damage without direct invasion.

mcqs.q: A patient with a history of extensive ileal resection for Crohn's disease develops severe vitamin B12 deficiency and chronic diarrhea. The diarrhea is most likely due to:
o: Bile salt malabsorption leading to colonic irritation.
Loss of the intrinsic factor-B12 receptor complex.
Increased bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine.
mcqs.e: Ileal resection disrupts the absorption of bile salts, which then enter the colon, causing osmotic diarrhea and irritation. The B12 deficiency is also due to loss of the ileal receptor, but the diarrhea is primarily from bile salt malabsorption.

mcqs.q: A 35-year-old pregnant woman in her second trimester presents with chronic diarrhea and weight loss. Stool studies confirm Giardia lamblia infection. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
mcqs.e: Metronidazole is generally considered safe and effective for giardiasis in the second and third trimesters of pregnancy. Albendazole and nitazoxanide are less preferred, and ivermectin is for Strongyloides.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a red-flag symptom in a patient with suspected malabsorption that mandates urgent referral?
o: Mild weight loss of 3% over 6 months.
mcqs.e: Severe electrolyte disturbances (e.g., hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia) indicate significant physiological derangement and can rapidly become life-threatening, requiring urgent medical attention.

mcqs.q: A patient with suspected malabsorption undergoes a D-xylose absorption test. A serum D-xylose level of 15 mg/dL at 1 hour is obtained. This result indicates:
mcqs.e: A serum D-xylose level <25 mg/dL at 1 hour indicates impaired mucosal absorptive capacity, as D-xylose is absorbed directly by the small intestinal mucosa without requiring pancreatic enzymes.

cases.v: A 28-year-old female presents to the clinic with a 3-month history of chronic, foul-smelling, bulky stools that are difficult to flush. She reports unintentional weight loss of 7 kg (15% of her body weight) during this period, along with generalized fatigue and abdominal bloating. She has no significant past medical history and denies recent travel. On examination, she appears thin, with evidence of muscle wasting. Her conjunctivae are pale. Abdominal examination reveals mild distension but no tenderness or organomegaly.

qs.q: What are the key clinical features suggesting malabsorption in this patient?
qs.a: The key features are chronic steatorrhea (foul-smelling, bulky, difficult-to-flush stools), significant unintentional weight loss (>10% in 3 months), generalized fatigue, abdominal bloating, muscle wasting, and pallor (suggesting anaemia).

qs.q: What initial investigations would you order to confirm malabsorption and identify potential causes, considering a low-resource setting?
qs.a: Initial investigations would include: 1) Stool microscopy for fat globules (Sudan III stain) and ova/cysts/parasites (e.g., Giardia). 2) Full blood count (for anaemia, microcytic/macrocytic). 3) Serum albumin (for protein status). 4) Electrolytes (to check for imbalances). 5) If available, a D-xylose absorption test to assess mucosal function. If not, consider a therapeutic trial for common causes like Giardia or tropical sprue.

qs.q: If her stool microscopy is negative for parasites but she has impaired D-xylose absorption, what would be your next diagnostic and management step?
qs.a: Impaired D-xylose absorption suggests mucosal disease. Given the context, tropical sprue is a strong possibility. The next step would be a therapeutic trial with broad-spectrum antibiotics (tetracycline) and folic acid. If there's a good clinical response, it supports the diagnosis of tropical sprue. If no response, further investigation like endoscopy with duodenal biopsy (if available) would be considered to rule out other mucosal pathologies.

cases.v: A 5-year-old child is brought to the hospital by his mother due to persistent poor weight gain, recurrent abdominal pain, and frequent loose, pale stools for the past 8 months. He is below the 3rd percentile for weight and height. His mother reports he often complains of 'tummy ache' after meals. Physical examination reveals a distended abdomen, thin limbs, and signs of vitamin A deficiency (Bitot's spots on conjunctivae). Stool microscopy shows numerous undigested fat globules.

qs.q: What is the most likely type of malabsorption in this child, and what specific nutrient deficiency is evident?
qs.a: The most likely type is fat malabsorption, indicated by undigested fat globules in stool and pale stools. The evident specific nutrient deficiency is vitamin A deficiency, manifested by Bitot's spots.

qs.q: Considering the child's age and presentation, what are the most probable causes of malabsorption in this low-resource setting?
qs.a: Probable causes include chronic parasitic infections (e.g., Giardia, Strongyloides), pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (e.g., due to cystic fibrosis, though rare, or severe malnutrition), tropical sprue, or less commonly, intestinal tuberculosis or HIV enteropathy.

qs.q: Outline the immediate management priorities for this child.
qs.a: Immediate priorities include: 1) Nutritional support: high-calorie, nutrient-dense diet, possibly with medium-chain triglycerides. 2) Supplementation of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and other micronutrients. 3) Treatment of underlying cause: empiric antiparasitic therapy (e.g., metronidazole) if Giardia is suspected, or broad-spectrum antibiotics if tropical sprue is considered. 4) Address dehydration and electrolyte imbalances if present. 5) Monitor weight gain and clinical improvement closely.

mistakes: Stating that >10% weight loss in 2 weeks is the threshold for rapid weight loss; the correct threshold is >5% in 6-12 months or >10% in 6 months.
Applying specific albumin cut-offs (e.g., <30 g/L for severe) as standard diagnostic criteria for staging malabsorption severity, rather than as indicators of protein loss.
Stating the cut-off for vitamin B12 deficiency as <150 pmol/L; the correct value is <148 pmol/L.
Claiming a specific Stage I, II, III system for malabsorption severity; no such standardized system is widely recognized.
Stating that HIV enteropathy often has CD4 <200 cells/µL; it can occur at any CD4 count.
Advising patients with pancreatic insufficiency to avoid high-fat meals; instead, PERT should be dosed appropriately for fat digestion.
exam: A 45-year-old female presents with persistent diarrhea, weight loss, and suspected malabsorption. A duodenal biopsy is stained with Congo red, showing orange-red deposits that display apple-green birefringence under polarized light. What is the most likely diagnosis? — This finding is pathognomonic for amyloidosis. Amyloid deposition in the small bowel can lead to malabsorption by interfering with mucosal integrity and function.

A 45-year-old man presents with chronic steatorrhea and abdominal pain. Endoscopic workup reveals exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. Which digestive enzyme deficiency is the primary cause of his lipid malabsorption? — Lipase deficiency is the primary cause of lipid malabsorption in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. Lipase is essential for breaking down triglycerides into absorbable fatty acids and monoglycerides.

A patient with an ileal resection develops severe vitamin B12 deficiency and bile salt malabsorption. Which specific transporter mechanism in the terminal ileum is disrupted by this surgical intervention? — The intrinsic factor-vitamin B12 receptor complex (also known as cubilin-amnionless complex) is disrupted, preventing B12 absorption. Additionally, the apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter (ASBT) is disrupted, leading to bile salt malabsorption.

A patient with fat malabsorption secondary to Crohn's disease exhibits areflexia and hemolytic anemia. Which fat-soluble vitamin acts primarily as an intracellular antioxidant? — Vitamin E (tocopherol) acts primarily as an intracellular antioxidant. Its deficiency can lead to neurological symptoms like areflexia and hemolytic anemia due to oxidative damage to red blood cell membranes.

A patient presents with chronic malabsorption and foul-smelling steatorrhea. Duodenal biopsy confirms Giardia lamblia infection. How does this parasite primarily induce malabsorption without invading the mucosal epithelium? — Giardia lamblia causes malabsorption by adhering to the brush border of the small intestine, forming a physical barrier. This interferes with nutrient absorption, damages microvilli, and can induce inflammation, leading to impaired enzyme function and increased permeability.

An infant who underwent a massive bowel resection for gangrenous intussusception develops severe malabsorption and fluid balance issues postoperatively. Which complication of surgical management is this infant most likely experiencing? — This infant is most likely experiencing short bowel syndrome. This condition results from extensive loss of small intestine, leading to inadequate surface area for nutrient and fluid absorption.

A 6-year-old child presents with chronic intermittent abdominal pain, malabsorption, and recurrent episodes of vomiting. An upper GI contrast study reveals that the duodenojejunal junction lies to the right of the midline. What is the most likely diagnosis? — This finding suggests intestinal malrotation. Malrotation can lead to chronic abdominal pain, malabsorption due to altered anatomy and potential intermittent volvulus, and recurrent vomiting.

A patient with systemic sclerosis presents with severe gastrointestinal dysmotility and malabsorption. What is the underlying histological change in the bowel wall? — The underlying histological change is fibrosis and atrophy of the smooth muscle layers, along with vascular changes and neural degeneration. This leads to impaired peristalsis and nutrient transit.

Distinguish between maldigestion and malabsorption in the context of chronic diarrhea. — Maldigestion is the impaired breakdown of nutrients into absorbable forms, often due to enzyme deficiencies (e.g., pancreatic insufficiency). Malabsorption is the impaired uptake of digested nutrients across the intestinal mucosa into the bloodstream or lymphatics (e.g., celiac disease).

A patient died following prolonged cholestasis. On post-mortem examination, the skin showed evidence of xanthomas and the gastrointestinal tract revealed signs of severe malabsorption. Explain the underlying mechanisms for malabsorption in this context. — Prolonged cholestasis leads to reduced bile flow into the intestine. Bile salts are crucial for emulsifying dietary fats and forming micelles, which are necessary for fat-soluble vitamin absorption. Their deficiency results in severe fat and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption.

In a post-mortem examination, you note signs of severe fat malabsorption in the gastrointestinal tract. Briefly describe the two primary functions of bile that are essential for normal digestion and excretion. — Bile's primary functions are: 1) Emulsification of dietary fats in the small intestine, increasing their surface area for enzymatic digestion by lipase. 2) Formation of micelles with digested fats and fat-soluble vitamins, facilitating their transport to the intestinal brush border for absorption. Bile also aids in cholesterol and bilirubin excretion.

A patient with chronic liver disease presented with generalized pruritus, pale stools, and dark urine prior to death. Post-mortem examination showed evidence of significant bile retention. What is the clinical term for this condition, and how does it relate to malabsorption? — The clinical term is cholestasis. Bile retention leads to a lack of bile salts in the intestine, impairing fat emulsification and micelle formation. This results in severe fat malabsorption, causing pale stools (steatorrhea) and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins.

What bedside clues would make you suspect malabsorption in a patient with chronic diarrhoea? — Key clues include chronic, often foul-smelling, fatty diarrhoea (steatorrhea), significant unintentional weight loss, abdominal bloating or distension, muscle wasting, and signs of specific nutrient deficiencies like pallor (anaemia), easy bruising (vitamin K), or night blindness (vitamin A).

How would you differentiate tropical sprue from Giardia infection using limited tests? — Stool microscopy for Giardia cysts/trophozoites is key for Giardia. If negative, a therapeutic trial of metronidazole for Giardia can be considered. For tropical sprue, a D-xylose absorption test showing impaired absorption, along with a good response to broad-spectrum antibiotics (tetracycline and folic acid), would support the diagnosis.
